vignette:
Javier used to find a quiet satisfaction in the predictable grid of a spreadsheet. For thirty years, his world was one of numbers, rules, and logic. As a tax consultant, he brought order to the financial chaos of his clients' lives, and in doing so, shored up the foundations of his own. Everything had a place, every debit a credit. He believed in the system. He believed that if you followed the rules, you were safe.

That belief shattered on a Tuesday night eighteen months ago. He was driving home from a late client meeting, his mind already organizing the documents for the next day. The flashing lights in his rearview mirror were an annoyance, not a threat. He'd discovered his right taillight was out that morning and had planned to fix it on the weekend. He pulled over, rolled down his window, and placed his hands on the steering wheel, just as he'd seen in movies.

He can't recall the exact sequence of events that followed, only a series of searing, disjointed snapshots. The officer's flashlight beam was blinding, dancing across his face. The questions were sharp, accusatory. He remembers the confusion, the rising panic in his chest as he tried to explain he was just coming from work. Then, another officer was at his passenger door, wrenching it open. There was shouting. He was being pulled from the car, his shoulder screaming in protest. The world became a dizzying mix of flashing lights, the rough texture of asphalt against his cheek, and the metallic taste of blood in his mouth. He remembers the crushing weight on his back and the cold, tight bite of handcuffs around his wrists. He never understood why. No explanation was ever given. He was released hours later with a dislocated shoulder, bruised ribs, and a citation for the broken taillight.

In the weeks that followed, Javier tried to file the incident away in a mental ledger labeled "bad luck." He told his wife, Maria, he was fine. He told his clients he'd slipped on some ice. He returned to his spreadsheets, seeking refuge in their familiar order. But the order was gone. The numbers would blur, and he'd see the strobing red and blue lights behind his eyelids. The scrape of a chair in the office would make him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were back on the pavement.

He stopped driving after dark. A police car, even blocks away, would send a wave of nausea and cold sweat through him. He started having nightmares-vivid, suffocating dreams of being pinned down, unable to breathe. He'd wake up tangled in his sheets, his jaw clenched so tight it ached for hours.

His work, once his sanctuary, became a source of profound anxiety. He couldn't concentrate, his mind constantly scanning for threats that weren't there. Deadlines were missed. Details were overlooked. The man who took pride in his meticulousness now felt like a fraud. He grew irritable and distant. Maria's attempts to comfort him felt like an intrusion. She would ask what was wrong, and a hot, inexplicable rage would well up inside him. He didn't have the words for the shame and the feeling of utter powerlessness that had taken root in his soul. The system he'd trusted had broken him without reason, and he couldn't make it make sense.

The divorce was finalized six months ago. Maria said she felt like she was living with a ghost. Now, he lives alone in an apartment that feels too quiet. He spends most of his time at his desk, staring at the screen, but the numbers no longer offer any comfort. They are just symbols, as meaningless as the rules he once believed would protect him. Sometimes, the siren of a passing ambulance will rise in the distance, and he will freeze, his hands gripping the edge of his desk, waiting for a danger that has already come and gone, and yet is always, somehow, still there.
